entries.text:
The canvas toolbar is one row of equal menus: "New console" becomes "Consoles",
and Fence and Note gain the same dropdown chevron.
entries.headline: The canvas toolbar reads as one row of equal menus

entries.text:
Claude consoles keep their transcripts when the daemon is restarted from inside
a Claude Code session. A running console restarts from its titlebar, and a
console in a locked fence shows the lock.
entries.headline: Claude consoles keep their transcripts across a daemon restart

entries.text:
The console's Paste key pastes a clipboard image (an iPhone screenshot, say) as a
clipboard drop, like a keyboard paste; before, it pasted text only.
entries.headline: The console's Paste key pastes a clipboard image

entries.text:
On a phone the canvas gets the screen: the console toolbar and Consoles tab show
icons only, and the Projects sidebar opens closed and slides over the canvas.
entries.headline: On a phone, the canvas gets the screen

entries.text:
The release page lists one line per capability, leaving a new feature's own
fixes to CHANGELOG.md, and the What's new panel reads its emoji headings.
entries.headline: Release notes are one line per feature, and the What's new panel reads them right

entries.text:
A console no longer hangs on "reconnecting…" after a phone resumes: a reconnect
whose handshake stalls is dropped after a few seconds and retried.
entries.headline: A console no longer hangs on "reconnecting…" after a phone resumes

entries.text:
The Projects sidebar names each environment once, shows peer connection as a
pair of plugs (click to wake one), counts changes only when there are some, and
puts the branch switcher on the open project's row.
entries.headline: The Projects sidebar reads at a glance

entries.text:
The workbench loads faster over a tunnel and reloads for free: every asset
carries a content ETag so a reload is a round of 304s, and text assets go out
gzipped (11 MB down to 3 MB on first open).

Open a console that starts straight into a command of your choice — `htop`,
`btop`, `lazygit`… Set it once under Settings → Consoles and it joins the New
console menu (Alt+Shift+9); the console closes when the command exits.

The workbench opens, searches and saves text in any encoding (Windows-1252, UTF-16, …), names it on the file tab with "reopen with…" and "save with…", and keeps a refused file's tab open with the reason instead of closing it.

Write a note on the consoles stage: markdown that renders as you type — Notion
style, with a slash menu, task lists and tables — autosaved into an opaque
`.note` file in the project you are working in. A note names its own file from
its first heading, picks a colour that travels with the file, opens links into
the workbench, and gives its editor back while it is off-screen.

A `.note` in the file explorer opens as its card on the consoles stage — and
jumps to it if the card is already there, rather than opening a second editor
over one file. The card can rename or delete its own file, and a note whose
file has gone says so and can be pointed at another one instead of quietly
disappearing.

A note card is written in a hand and a size of your choosing — sans, serif or
mono, in five steps — chosen from the palette and kept in the file, so a note
comes back in its own hand when you open it again. The file's own menu moved
out of the card's titlebar into a gear in the footer, beside the path it acts
on, and hiding a note is the eye's job alone now.

The Note menu is a map: every note on the plane is a row that slides the view
to its card, and a note's own `##` sections hang under it — collapsed — so a
long note is one click from the part you meant.

A ```mermaid fence inside a note draws the diagram, and clicking it opens a
small editor over the drawing with a live preview — Ctrl+Enter applies,
Esc cancels. Mermaid diagrams also get their labels back everywhere in the
workbench, including the file viewer: the sanitizer had been removing them.

A note can be marked to open hidden: the eye in the card's head writes the mark
and shows the note for this session only, and a hidden card mounts no editor at
all — the text is never put on the page, just the eye in the middle of it.
A guard against the room rather than encryption; the file is obfuscated, not
secret.

Open a second file beside the one you are reading, or mirror the same file
into a second editor with its own scroll and cursor; the arrangement follows
this browser across reloads.
The Changes panel now names the worktree it reads, with the same chip and picker as the Files bar, so the selected tree is visible without leaving the panel.

The Changes panel shows when a fetch, pull or push is still running: the busy
button spins and the remote bar locks until the upstream answers, so a slow
push no longer looks like a dead click.

A console comes back after a network switch or a long stretch in the background,
even behind a tunnel, instead of closing or asking you to take it over.

After a daemon restart, an old console window can no longer reattach to a different
session, and the restarted daemon keeps writing to `daemon.log`.

The New console menu is a launcher again: every row opens a new console on
click (the live count stays as a readout), the head names the repo by its bare
name, and the accelerator pattern is stated once with each row carrying only
its digit.

The workbench no longer keeps a password field in the page when nothing is
asking for a password: the login gate's and the settings modal's are rendered
only while those surfaces are open. Typing in any other field — renaming a note,
for one — stopped making the browser offer to save what you typed as a password.

A note card can be typed into wherever it sits: a card restored beside a
console was drawn under it and the keystrokes went to the shell. The card also
wears the plane's own chrome now instead of text glyphs, its title is renamed
by clicking it, and its ground and its text colour are chosen separately — a
solid tone with a light ink is a yellow note with white writing on it.

A note card is a card, not a page. Its editor's toolbar and slash menu are
sized for a 320 px note instead of a full document and their icons are drawn in
a colour you can see; headings look like headings again; bullets, numbers and
task checkboxes appear at all; the `+`/`⠿` block handle that had nowhere to sit
is gone (`/` opens the same menu); a click on the blank space below the last
line keeps the caret instead of dropping the next keystrokes; and pressing
Enter reads as the next line rather than a gap. A note's title now lives in the
file's header instead of being repeated as a heading at the top of the body —
existing notes keep their name and are migrated the first time you rename one.
A mermaid diagram applies what you typed into it, says so when it is still
empty, and no longer leaves its error cartoon on the plane.

Picking a section from a note's index scrolls the note to it and leaves the
canvas where it was — the plane no longer pans out from under the card.

Links in a note are typed, readable, and reachable: `[text](url)` and the
`@@path/to/file` shorthand now make one as you type, a link follows the card's
own ink instead of a fixed colour that was unreadable on a filled card, and the
hover preview no longer prints the path in the card's ink on the plane's dark
chrome. A card's footer also says when the note was last saved, and the close
toast names the file once.

A note's lock pins the card in place and nothing more — a locked note is still
typed into, renamed, recoloured and hidden; only moving and resizing are
refused. The eye is on every card now, so hiding a note is one press instead of
a trip through the file menu. And a card whose file cannot be read keeps what
you had typed on screen instead of blanking, while a note's path is recorded
only once its first save has actually landed — a write that never lands no
longer leaves a card pointing at a file nobody created.

A note card says what to type: the footer's gear → `Markdown help` lists the
marks the editor understands (CommonMark + GFM, including a ```mermaid fence that draws), `[ ]`
on a plain line now makes a task instead of literal text, the head gained an
index of the note's `##` headings, an empty heading reads "Write a title", the
scrollbar fades out when the card is not in use, and a new note is born in the
operator's colours.

A mermaid diagram in a note is drawn on the card instead of in a dark box cut
out of it: its nodes, edges and labels are mixed from the card's own ground and
ink, so it reads on any tone — and restyling the note repaints the diagrams in
it.

Notes keep what you typed: the last character before a close, a `Ctrl+S` or a
tab closing is no longer lost to the editor's own change notification arriving
late, two saves of one card can no longer land out of order, and a note is
named once instead of leaving an orphan file behind. A note also opens where
the card can be used — in edit, outside any fence, centred by the map — and the
card's file menu no longer hangs open over the text.
Keeping a WSL distro awake no longer opens an empty `wsl.exe` terminal tab on Windows.

A WSL peer stays up: the Windows daemon now holds its distro awake — at start
and on every nudge — so a console on a WSL project no longer closes half a
minute after the peer wakes.

Closes the 2026-09 security audit: workbench file writes can no longer reach
`.git` or `.ralphy` under any spelling, issue comments from non-collaborators
no longer reach the agent, and lowering your own login posture now costs a
fresh factor.

The console works from a phone: a maximized console takes the whole screen, the
key bar gains paste and a drag-to-select-lines mode, and copy wears a copy icon.

Lock a console or a fence in place from its title bar so a slipped finger on a
tablet cannot move it, and a tap on a title bar no longer counts as a drag.

A desk full of consoles stays fast: a console scrolled well off the viewport
puts its terminal to sleep and gives its renderer back, and repaints from the
daemon's scrollback the moment it comes into view again.

A console no longer comes back twice when the workbench is open on more than
one device: a page merges the desk with what the other pages saved before it
writes, and a session whose record lost its id returns to its own window
instead of a new one beside it.

The workbench reads on a phone: a file's toolbar names only its path, its
controls stay reachable, a Markdown document's index folds into an overlay you
open when you want it, an issue on the board opens across the whole pane
with a back arrow instead of a close button that had scrolled out of reach,
and a console's title bar and the board's header stay one row with their
close buttons in reach.

An execute session no longer pays for a second self-review after fixing the
first one's HIGH findings: the fix is proved by the scoped test and the green
gate, not by re-running the reviewer over the same diff.

The branch picker lists the project's worktrees under `.ralphy/worktrees/` —
name, branch and a dirty dot, with the primary tree first — and `ralphy
worktree list` prints the same listing at the shell.

The branch picker creates a worktree by name on its own branch from the
current one (gitignored files are not copied), and `ralphy worktree add <name>
[--base <ref>]` does the same at the shell — both refused while a run holds
the repo.

Pick a worktree in the branch picker and the project's Files tree, file
viewer and Find read from it, the branch chip names it, and the choice is
remembered across reloads and browsers.

With a worktree picked, the Changes panel, the diff and the branch chip act on
that worktree: stage, commit, discard, diff and branch switches land there,
and the primary tree is untouched.

Open a console inside the worktree picked in the branch picker, for every
agent: it works there, its title says so, and it stays there when you pick
another tree. The experimental `console_worktree` key in `repos.toml` (the
`claude --worktree` trial) is retired — it still loads, is ignored, and is
reported once.

Remove a worktree from the branch picker (or `ralphy worktree remove <name>`):
refused while a console lives in it, while it is locked or has uncommitted
changes; the directory goes, and the branch is deleted only when git agrees
it is fully merged — otherwise it is kept and you are told why.

When a project has worktrees, the worktree named in a console's title is a
switcher: pick another tree and the console restarts there.

A console, its project and its worktree show when the agent is working, done,
or waiting for you — and the Telegram card buzzes with what it is asking.

`ralphy daemon install` registers a launchd agent on macOS, so the daemon
starts at login there as it already does on Windows and Linux. On a Windows
without PowerShell 7 the registration now runs under Windows PowerShell
instead of pointing at an interpreter that is not there.

Push from the Changes panel (and `ralphy sync push`) now publishes whichever
branch you are on, the repo's default branch included — the remote's own branch
protection is the only gate.

The login card offers *Keep me signed in*: an opt-in session that survives a
closed browser (7 days idle, 30 days absolute). Logging out anywhere still ends it.

A new worktree can carry the primary tree's gitignored files with it: list
what to copy (`.env`) and what to link (`node_modules`) under `worktree` in
`.ralphy/settings.json`.

A console moves into a worktree — or cuts a new one — from its own title bar
and restarts there; the Files bar shows which tree you are looking at, and
the branch picker is about branches again.

The Spend view attributes a worktree console's tokens to its project: a
session that ran inside `.ralphy/worktrees/<name>` no longer shows up
unattributed.

A console opened in a worktree comes back in that worktree after the daemon
restarts, and says so if the worktree is gone instead of quietly reopening in
the primary tree.

A project registered before it had a GitHub remote is shown as `owner/repo` as soon as the remote exists — the Board, Spend, Runs and Settings stop printing its `path-…` hash, its consoles, usage and event settings follow it, and no second sidebar entry appears for the same directory.

A worktree that shares a directory such as `node_modules` from the primary tree is clean on Linux and macOS as it already was on Windows: the link is excluded locally, so the tree no longer reads dirty, can be removed, and a commit never picks the link up.

The file tree no longer paints its rows a third of the way down a blank panel
after an agent writes files, and a folder refreshed while its parent is being
re-listed no longer reports "Could not refresh the file list (null is not an
object …)". A screenshot paste that the daemon drops without a reply now says
why, on both the console and the daemon log.
Workbench help text, confirmation dialogs and Spend notes are shorter and plainer: one or two direct sentences, no engineering asides, easier to read for non-native English speakers.
A link in a rendered markdown document opens the file it names in the workbench: another document as a new reading tab, source as an editor tab.
The FILES panel gains a search field (Ctrl+Shift+F): type part of a file name, or switch to Content to look inside files, and the tree narrows to the matches.
Filtering the project list no longer blanks the open project's file tree when the search is cleared.
A Claude console is only renamed to `wb-<repo>-<hex>` when the project turns on `claude.console_name`; left off, Claude names each session itself.
`ralphy update --check` tells you whether your build is behind what is published, and lists every release in between.
The daemon checks the published releases every six hours and reports the gap at `GET /api/release`. A marker file in the daemon store turns it off.
`ralphy update` installs the newest release: the archive for your platform, refused unless its checksum matches, then the daemon restarted onto it.
The workbench dots the account puck when a newer build is out, with a What's new panel listing what each release in the gap changed.
A project whose working tree could not be read now shows the reason on hover in its changes badge, instead of the generic label.
On a tablet, the key bar no longer covers a console's bottom-right corner, so the resize grip is back where a finger reaches for it.
Reloading the workbench from a tab other than Consoles no longer moves every restored console to the top-left corner.
The Explorer no longer shows a folder that isn't there: a directory recreated under a name that was just used lists its own contents, not the old one's.
`ralphy install --force` can now replace a `ralphy` that is currently running — the resident daemon being the ordinary case.
Release machinery: the fold refuses to re-fold a version whose fragments it consumed, `bump` refuses a version Cargo would reject, and `ralphy update` restarts the daemon it actually installed over.
Settings drops the Schedule section and the queue's "Eligible labels" field, which were never wired to anything; the fallback verify command is now shown read-only.
